items.description: Context-engineering primitives for Artificial Intelligence (AI) coding agents working in R. Assembles agent context from memory and instruction files ('AGENTS.md', 'CLAUDE.md'), traces function call blast radius across projects, generates project briefings, parses source into Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) symbol indices, discovers dependency graphs, and introspects installed packages. Zero dependencies.
title: saber: Context Engineering for Large Language Model Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents operating on long-running tasks inevitably exceed their usable context window, forcing a choice about what history to discard. In practice, most agent frameworks default to one of two simple strategies: dropping the oldest turns, or replacing them with an LLM-generated summary. A third strategy, retrieving only the turns most relevant to the current query regardless of age, is common in retrieval-augmented systems but is rarely compared head-to-head against the first two under a controlled, fact-recall task. We introduce a synthetic long-context recall task in which specific facts (random codes, names, dates) are planted at known positions within a long sequence of conversational turns, and an agent must answer questions about both early-planted and recently-planted facts after its context has been compressed to a fixed budget. We compare three context-management strategies: dropoldest, summarize-oldest, and keep-most-relevant, using real calls to a production LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6), grading each answer automatically against a known gold value. Across 20 independent trials (360 graded queries), summarize-oldest achieves 94.2% overall recall accuracy, keep-most-relevant achieves 60.0%, and drop-oldest achieves only 41.7% (χ 2 = 75.17, p &lt; 0.00001). The effect is driven almost entirely by facts stated early in the conversation: drop-oldest recalls 0% of early-stated facts (Fisher's exact test vs. both alternatives, p &lt; 0.00001), confirming that its failures are not occasional misses but a complete, systematic loss of any information outside the retained recency window. Summarize-oldest retains 90.4% accuracy on these same early facts despite paying only one additional LLM call per compression event, while keep-most-relevant, using a deliberately weak, local, non-semantic embedding, partially but incompletely recovers early facts (61.5%). We discuss the practical implications for agent framework design and the limitations of our synthetic, single-model, single-budget setup.</jats:p>
title: An Empirical Evaluation of Context-Management Strategies for Large Language Model Agents Under Forced Context Compression

project-title.title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Adaptive Cooperative Agents

project-description.description:
Notre vie quotidienne est remplie de nombreuses interactions coopératives multi-agents. Cela inclut nos activités quotidiennes régulières telles que traverser un feu de circulation, conduire, acheter et vendre des biens et services, ainsi que nos activités dans les écoles, les bureaux et les gouvernements, pour n'en nommer que quelques-unes. Les agents et systèmes d’intelligence artificielle (IA) sont très prometteurs pour nous assister dans bon nombre de ces activités quotidiennes. Il est primordial que ces agents IA aient la capacité de se coordonner avec plusieurs humains et autres agents (IA ou autres), en particulier avec un nombre croissant de robots IA déployés dans le monde réel, y compris les voitures autonomes. Construire de tels agents d'IA est un défi, car une coopération réussie nécessite qu'un agent anticipe les comportements des autres agents.

Il y a eu récemment un regain d'intérêt au sein de la communauté de recherche en IA pour la création d'agents coopératifs d'apprentissage par renforcement multi-agents (MARL). En particulier, la communauté s'est principalement concentrée sur la conception de méthodes permettant aux agents RL formés d'effectuer une coordination Zero-Shot (ZSC) avec de nouveaux agents invisibles, y compris nos travaux (Nekoei, et al. 2021).

Nous avons constaté que se concentrer uniquement sur la coordination Zero-Shot (ZSC) pour les agents coopératifs d'apprentissage par renforcement multi-agents (MARL) est limitant. Pour résoudre ce problème, nous avons introduit un benchmark de coordination en quelques étapes (Nekoei, et al., 2023) et découvert que les méthodes ZSC actuelles nécessitent des millions d'interactions avec de nouveaux partenaires pour parvenir à une coordination satisfaisante. Cela soulève notre question centrale de recherche : comment pouvons-nous concevoir des méthodes MARL qui combinent des principes généraux de coopération avec des politiques adaptatives pour de nouveaux scénarios ?

D'autre part, les grands modèles linguistiques (LLM) représentent des modèles de texte génératifs formés sur de vastes ensembles de données collectés sur Internet, dotés de la capacité de prédire le jeton suivant dans une séquence en fonction d'indices contextuels. Les LLM modernes tels que ChatGPT ont présenté des capacités remarquables de généralisation à zéro ou à quelques coups, en particulier dans des tâches complexes telles que le raisonnement et l'arithmétique. Compte tenu des progrès notables dans le développement des LLM, une question immédiate et impérieuse se pose : pouvons-nous exploiter les capacités des LLM et les connaissances approfondies en matière d'interaction humaine qu'ils contiennent pour fournir un soutien non seulement aux agents MARL dans un contexte général, mais aussi, spécifiquement, pour Agents coopératifs Hanabi?

Dans ce projet, nous proposons de travailler vers les trois objectifs de recherche suivants : 1- Évaluer les LLM actuels sur leur capacité à coopérer en comprenant l'intention des autres LLM et en utilisant efficacement la théorie de l'esprit. 2- Utiliser les connaissances générales et le bon sens du LLM pour former des agents RL généralistes. 3- Tirez parti des capacités de raisonnement en quelques étapes du LLM pour vous adapter rapidement à de nouveaux partenaires au moment du test.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Flexible building loads can reduce costs and relieve power networks, but fleet control must coordinate heterogeneous devices without creating demand peaks, comfort violations, or feeder overload. Large language model (LLM) agents promise adaptable, zero-shot control, but their operational value remains unclear because comparisons with trained numerical controllers rarely use matched trajectories or consistently account for uncertainty and inference cost. We address this gap with DRBENCH, a commonevaluation frameworkfor rule-based control, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning (RL), coordinated and residual RL, and three LLM-agent designs. The framework couples building and device dynamics through a shared feeder, evaluates methods on identical episodes with paired statistics, measures inference overhead, and examines transfer to CityLearn data. The findingsshow that flexible language reasoning alone does not produce effective real-time dispatch. In the synthetic evaluation, PPO and SAC outperform all evaluated online LLM agents on cost and peak control and avoid the observed feeder overloads. Direct LLM control increases the weekly bill by $309 relative to PPO, while online LLM decisions are 1,000–10,000 times slower than learned-policy inference. Residual RL gives the strongest mean performance, indicating that learning benefits from refining a structured control prior. CityLearn provides an important qualification: direct and ReAct agents improve on a fixed time-of-use rule but not on MPC, and RL is not evaluated in that setting. Overall, the evidence supports numerical controllers for operational dispatch and positions LLMs more credibly as offline aids for specification, reward design, and controller configuration.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The present study aimed to 1) investigate beliefs about language learning, language learning strategies, proficiency, gender, and educational context of Thai upper secondary school students and 2) propose the model of relationships between the five variables. The participants were 458 twelfth grade students in Bangkok, academic year 2013. The data were collected by means of a questionnaire. The data analysis consisted of descriptive statistics and structural equation modeling (SEM) to analyze the model of relationships. Findings revealed that Thai upper secondary school students hold beliefs about language learning in terms of the special ability for language learning in some individuals. They viewed English as moderately difficult and emphasized the cultures of the English-speakers, vocabulary learning, and good accent. They also believed that having good speaking skills leads to better job opportunities. The use of language learning strategies was at the moderate level. In this study, most of the participants had high proficiency. There were more female than male students. And the two educational contexts in focus were regular programs using Thai as a medium of instruction and English programs using English. The structural equation model revealed the statistically significant direct effect of educational context on beliefs about language learning and the direct effect of beliefs about language learning on proficiency. The following goodness of fit was achieved: CMIN/DF = 1.42, p = .012, CFI = .983, RMSEA = .031, GFI = .972, AGFI = .957, and Hoelter = 417.</jats:p>
title: A MODEL OF RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN BELIEFS ABOUT LANGUAGE LEARNING, LANGUAGE LEARNING STRATEGIES, PROFICIENCY, GENDER, AND EDUCATIONAL CONTEXT OF THAI UPPER SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS
